antiPatterns.scenario: Do not show a Button that combines multiple outcomes.
Do not use competing Primary Buttons in the same action group.
Do not separate the Button from the content, decision, or consequence it controls.
Do not use more than one icon to reinforce the meaning of the button.

iOS / Android.animation:
The Button must provide immediate feedback when pressed.
Product-specific transitions, durations, easing, haptics, background changes, or border changes must be documented in UI or motion specifications.
Tap triggers the Pressed state visual (background / border tint change). On iOS the press-to-release transition follows UIKit defaults; on Android it includes the Material ripple.
iOS / Android.conditionalLogic:
The Button supports three states: Default, Pressed, Disabled.
Default is used when the action is available.
Pressed is used only while the user is actively pressing the Button.
Disabled is used when the action is unavailable, incomplete, blocked, or not allowed.
When disabled, the Button is still visible (greyed out) but not interactive.
iOS / Android.copyAndTruncation:
Keep labels short (1–3 words) to avoid wrapping in compact containers and to stay readable on small viewports. 
The Button label is mandatory.
Use short, action-oriented labels.
The label must describe the outcome of the action.
Use one action per Button label.
Avoid vague labels when the result is not clear from context.
Do not use explanatory text inside the Button.
Move conditions, warnings, or explanations outside the Button.
The Button label should remain on one line.
If the label does not fit, use a shorter label or adapt the layout.
If large font scaling causes overflow, consider reducing font size.
iOS / Android.interactiveElements:
The entire Button area is interactive.
The label and icons are part of the same touch target area.
Icons inside a Button reinforce the action but must not introduce a second action.
A Disabled Button is visible (greyed out) but not interactive.
iOS / Android.position:
Place the Button close to the content, decision, or flow step it acts on. 
In an inline Button Group, place the Primary Button on the trailing side.
Place Secondary or Ghost actions on the leading side when they appear next to a Primary Button.
iOS / Android.size:
The Button touch target must meet platform accessibility requirements.
iOS: minimum hit area of 44×44 pt.
Android / Material: minimum touch target of 48×48 dp.
The visible Button size may be smaller only if the effective interactive area still meets the platform minimum.

commonPatterns.description:
The Button is an interactive control that allows the user to trigger an action, submit a decision, start a process, or confirm an intent. It exists to make actionable choices clear, recognizable, and easy to activate across different product flows. 

The Button component is defined by two independent decision axes: 
Hierarchy: defines the visual weight of the action within the screen:
Primary: the single main action of the screen or action context.
Secondary: an alternative, supporting, or equal-weight side action next to a Primary.
Ghost: a low-impact contextual action, such as Skip, Later, Show more, or similar non-blocking actions.
 For all the status described above, an icon can be actived (left or right). 
Appearance: defines the semantic context of the action:
Brand: product-level CTAs, such as Confirm, Continue, or Play.
Neutral: standard actions, technical actions, or settings-related actions, such as Save or Apply.
Accent: emphasised secondary actions that need more visibility without becoming the main action.
Danger: irreversible, destructive, or high-risk actions, such as Delete account or Cancel order.
Inverse: buttons placed on dark surfaces where the standard appearance would not provide the correct contextual contrast.
Use a Button to trigger one clear action.
In inline Button Groups, place the Primary action on the trailing side.
Place the Button close to the content or decision it acts on.
Use only one icon to reinforce the meaning of the button.

usedIn:
Form submission and confirmation flows.
Step-by-step flows where the user advances, confirms, or cancels.
Modal, dialog, or bottom-sheet actions.
Card or content-area actions.
Settings and preference management.
Transactional flows requiring explicit user intent.
Destructive or high-risk flows that need clear semantic emphasis.
Product-level CTAs that drive the main user task.
